n_plus_one_queries: N+1 query pattern: per-product round-trips for reviews and inventory

hypothesis.title: N+1 query pattern: per-product round-trips for reviews and inventory
hypothesis.explanation: The category_products function executes 1 query to verify the category, 1 query to fetch products (≈40 per category), then for EACH product: 1 query for reviews (rating_avg, review_count) and 1 query for inventory (stock). That's ~82 round-trips per request. At 93 req/s this generates ~7,600 queries/s, saturating the connection pool and DB CPU.
supporting_evidence: app/catalog.py lines 28-48: explicit loop with two await _query_row calls per product
db/schema.sql: 40 products per category (2000 products / 50 categories)
Baseline: DB CPU 97-106%, app CPU 105-121%, throughput only 93 req/s with 100 users
missing_evidence: Direct measurement of queries per request and transactions per second

proposed_experiment.rationale: If N+1 is the driver, each HTTP request will spawn ~80 'db.query' spans and DB will show ~7,500 transactions/sec. If false (e.g., queries are batched), we'll see ~3 spans/request and ~300 transactions/sec.

predictions.if_supported: N+1 pattern confirmed as primary latency source
predictions.if_refuted: Queries are already batched; look elsewhere

predictions.if_supported: DB throughput dominated by per-product round-trips
predictions.if_refuted: Transaction rate matches request rate; N+1 not the issue

events.message: connection_pool_exhaustion: Connection pool too small (max=20) for 100 concurrent users causing acquisition queuing

hypothesis.title: Connection pool too small (max=20) for 100 concurrent users causing acquisition queuing
hypothesis.explanation: The pool is configured with max_size=20 (db.py). With 100 concurrent users each holding a connection for the duration of ~80 serial queries, most requests wait for a free connection. This adds queueing latency on top of query time.
supporting_evidence: Baseline: 100 concurrent users, DB CPU ~100% (could be context-switching overhead from many active connections)
contradicting_evidence: If N+1 is true, pool exhaustion is a symptom not root cause; fixing N+1 would reduce connection hold time 20x
missing_evidence: Actual connection utilization and wait events during load

proposed_experiment.rationale: If pool exhaustion is the independent bottleneck, db_activity will show max connections pinned at 20 with high 'ClientRead' wait events (waiting for client) or 'ClientWrite' even after N+1 is mitigated. If false, max connections will stay well below 20.

predictions.observation: db_activity.active_connections.max == 20 AND db_activity.wait_events shows significant 'ClientRead'/'ClientWrite' time
predictions.if_supported: Pool saturation adds independent queuing latency
predictions.if_refuted: Pool not saturated; connection wait not a factor

events.message: database_cpu_saturation: Database CPU at 100% limits query throughput regardless of query count

hypothesis.title: Database CPU at 100% limits query throughput regardless of query count
hypothesis.explanation: The database container shows 97-106% CPU. If the DB is compute-bound (e.g., sequential scans, lack of indexes, or just raw query volume), it cannot process queries faster, causing queueing in PostgreSQL. This would manifest as high active connections with 'CPU' pressure (low wait-event time, high active time).
supporting_evidence: Baseline: db CPU 97-106% across three runs
Throughput plateau at ~93 req/s despite 100 users
contradicting_evidence: Schema has indexes on products.category_id, reviews.product_id, inventory.product_id PK
If N+1 is true, DB CPU is high because of query volume, not per-query cost
missing_evidence: Wait event breakdown showing whether connections are actively executing vs waiting

proposed_experiment.rationale: If DB CPU saturation is the fundamental limit, db_activity.wait_events will show minimal wait time (connections mostly 'active' not waiting) and transactions/sec will plateau even if we reduce query count. If false, wait events will show I/O or lock contention, or CPU will drop when query count drops.

predictions.observation: db_activity.wait_events shows >80% time in 'active' (no wait event) AND container_resources.db.cpu_percent stays >90% even if query count is reduced
predictions.if_supported: DB compute capacity is the hard ceiling
predictions.if_refuted: DB has headroom; latency comes from queueing/round-trips not raw CPU

key_observations: Measured 7146.7 DB transactions/sec at 93.5 req/s = 76.4 transactions/request, matching the predicted ~80 (1 category check + 1 product list + 40 products × 2 queries each = 82)
Individual db.query spans are fast (p50 0.8 ms, p99 2.0 ms) but the sheer volume (~76 round-trips/request) explains the HTTP p99 of 128.3 ms
Connection pool is NOT saturated (active connections avg 0.53, max 1 of 20), contradicting the 'saturating the connection pool' clause of the hypothesis
DB wait events show only Client:ClientRead (network/driver) and CPU:running — no lock or I/O contention visible
conclusion.explanation: The transaction-rate measurement (7146.7/s) matches the N+1 prediction (~7,600/s) almost exactly, confirming the per-product round-trip pattern as the dominant source of latency. The connection-pool saturation claim is false, but the core mechanism — 76+ sequential queries per request — is validated and sufficient to explain the SLO violation.

events.message: Root cause: N+1 query pattern: per-product round-trips for reviews and inventory

single_join_query: Replace the N+1 query pattern with a single aggregated JOIN query (plus the category existence check). The query joins products with a pre-aggregated reviews subquery and inventory in one round-trip, using LEFT JOINs to preserve products without reviews or inventory rows.

candidate.name: single_join_query
candidate.strategy: Replace the N+1 query pattern with a single aggregated JOIN query (plus the category existence check). The query joins products with a pre-aggregated reviews subquery and inventory in one round-trip, using LEFT JOINs to preserve products without reviews or inventory rows.
candidate.expected_effect: Reduces database round-trips from ~82 per request to 2 (category check + main query). Eliminates the per-product loop and its associated Python overhead. Expected p99 well below 50 ms because the dominant latency component (76 sequential round-trips) is removed.
candidate.risks: The JOIN query plan must use indexes efficiently (products.category_id, reviews.product_id, inventory.product_id). A poor plan (e.g., sequential scan on reviews) could increase per-query latency. The subquery grouping by product_id must correctly handle products with zero reviews (LEFT JOIN + COALESCE ensures review_count=0, rating_avg=NULL). Banker's rounding (ROUND_HALF_UP) is still applied in Python to match exact test expectations.

events.message: batch_queries_with_in: Keep the category check and product list as separate queries, but replace the per-product review and inventory queries with two batch queries using WHERE product_id = ANY($1). Fetch all review aggregates and all inventory rows for the product IDs in the category in two round-trips, then combine in Python using dictionaries.

candidate.name: batch_queries_with_in
candidate.strategy: Keep the category check and product list as separate queries, but replace the per-product review and inventory queries with two batch queries using WHERE product_id = ANY($1). Fetch all review aggregates and all inventory rows for the product IDs in the category in two round-trips, then combine in Python using dictionaries.
candidate.expected_effect: Reduces round-trips from ~82 to 4 (category check, products, batch reviews, batch inventory). The batch queries use indexed lookups (reviews.product_id, inventory.product_id) and return at most 40 rows each. Expected p99 well below 50 ms because the sequential per-product loop is eliminated.
candidate.risks: The ANY($1) array parameter must be correctly encoded by asyncpg (supported in asyncpg 0.30+). An empty product list is handled early to avoid empty array issues. The batch queries must use GROUP BY product_id for reviews and simple lookup for inventory. Dictionary merging in Python adds negligible overhead. Banker's rounding preserved.

events.message: jsonb_aggregation: Use PostgreSQL's JSONB functions (jsonb_build_object + jsonb_agg) to construct the complete product listing as a single JSON array in one query (plus the category check). The database returns a ready-to-use Python list[dict] via asyncpg's JSONB decoder. Banker's rounding is applied in a final Python loop to guarantee bit-for-bit compatibility with the original rounding mode.

The database returns a ready-to-use Python list[dict] via asyncpg's JSONB decoder. candidate.expected_effect: Reduces round-trips to 2 (category check + JSON aggregation query). The JSON aggregation query does all joins and aggregation server-side and returns a single JSONB value (~8 KB for 40 products). Network overhead and per-row Python object construction are minimized. Expected p99 well below 50 ms.
candidate.risks: Relies on asyncpg's JSONB type decoder returning native Python list/dict (standard in asyncpg 0.30+). If the decoder is missing, the result would be a JSON string requiring json.loads(). The query uses COALESCE(jsonb_agg(...), '[]'::jsonb) to handle empty categories. Rounding is done in Python after decoding to match ROUND_HALF_UP exactly. The JSONB construction adds CPU work on the DB side but avoids 80 round-trips.
